cells.tense: You are tending something that matters, and the ending it needs is already in view.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Clear away the finished task — close it, hand it off, put it down. Then leave the unfinished work untouched until tomorrow and watch it hold without you.
cells.core:
You can tell what's finished from what isn't, and you're not fighting the difference. Something in your care is reaching its natural end, and you're letting that be true without making it a loss. That's why the thing is still growing instead of stalling. The ending you're allowing and the care you've given are the same motion.

The work this asks of you is light once you name it. Look at what you're tending and find the part that's already done. Then finish touching it — take your hands off it on purpose, and see what holds. Because you've done the earlier part of this well, it does not need to be pried from you. Set down what's finished and the clearing mostly takes care of itself.
cells.sheetLine: You can let what's finished be finished.
cells.verb: tending what's growing and keeping it alive through what it's becoming
cells.place: where something has to end and be cleared before the next thing can start

cells.tense: You are bracing for endings that haven't arrived yet, tidying rooms nobody has left.
cells.act: dream the next step and take it
cells.ask: Name something you expect will end within a few months and see it finished, on a plain morning. Then do nothing about it that week, and once more. No list, no announcement.
cells.core:
You know endings are coming, and so you're reading the end before the story reaches it. Things get cleared early — a project let go the week it started, a person's role set aside before anyone asked. From the kitchen this is taking the pleasure out of what's still alive, and the people it holds notice nothing is allowed to run its course.

Let the future happen to you instead of drafting it. Take a thing you think will end and feel it already over, on an ordinary Tuesday, no speech and no list. Then leave it alone that week. Nothing gets cleared or saved; you find out how it lands when you've stopped holding it at arm's length. What you end after that keeps its own timing, and there's nothing left to brace against.
cells.sheetLine: You're clearing before anything has had a chance to run.
cells.verb: tending what's growing and keeping it alive through what it's becoming
cells.place: where something has to end and be cleared before the next thing can start

cells.tense: You were caretaking something that has already ended, and you are still tending it.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin a fresh thing this week with nothing behind it besides wanting to — a walk, a page, a skill. Keep it aimless for three days and see whether you like it.
cells.core:
Something you were tending has stopped, and your hands haven't gotten the news. The routine is still there. You still show up where care used to matter, doing the motions a finished thing no longer needs, and the effort goes nowhere. You are keeping a door open that already closed.

Put the energy somewhere it can actually catch. Begin a fresh thing you want to do, on purpose, before you have any reason to be good at it — that spark is the whole step. Nothing here asks you to end the old thing by force. You don't have to declare anything over or tell anyone. The old spot simply becomes the place the new thing happens, and the aimless three days show you how much you want it.

cells.tense: This ending is being made by you, and you are not counting it as yours.
cells.act: govern by knowing what to surrender
cells.ask: Whenever you quietly stop keeping something up, note what you're ending, in your head, before you do it. Then end it or don't. Just know it was you.
cells.core:
Something is being brought to a close by careful, patient attention — no announcement, no hard line, just the quiet decision not to keep it going. Asked about it, you'd say it petered out. The ending is being done with skill, by you, and the skill is the part you don't see as yours.

Stand beside the act once. When you're about to let something lapse, stop long enough to register what you're ending. Then let it end, or start it up again — either is fine, and nothing about the decision changes. What changes is who's holding the pen. The authority you're already using becomes something you can name as your own, and endings stop happening at you.
cells.sheetLine: You're quietly ending this, and calling it drift.
cells.verb: tending what's growing and keeping it alive through what it's becoming
cells.place: where something has to end and be cleared before the next thing can start

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is 'too many things at once' — the record only gives a future-braced posture bracing against endings it expects to have to author, not an inventory of commitments. A reader could reasonably say it's plain exhaustion or one hard situation, not over-tending; so the Too Much cell names the clearing before it's needed, which the record does support. The asks survive being wrong because each is one visible act anyone can do in a week regardless of whether my read is right. The sentence that serves me more than the person is 'You can tell the difference in five minutes' — a flattering promise about their own perception, so I cut it.
